s0.title: Give OpsWatch its own AWS identity
s0.purpose: OpsWatch needs an identity whose only right is to assume the read-only roles you will create in the next steps.

tabs.server: OpsWatch runs on my computer or a server (Docker)
tabs.aws: OpsWatch runs on AWS (ECS or EC2)

server.i1: Sign in to the AWS console of the account where you want to keep OpsWatch's identity. It can be the account you will monitor.
server.i2: Open IAM → Users → "Create user". Name it opswatch. Leave "Provide user access to the AWS Management Console" unchecked, then click "Next".
server.i3: On "<ui>Set permissions</ui>", keep "<ui>Add user to group</ui>" or choose "<ui>Attach policies directly</ui>" without selecting any policy. Click "<ui>Next</ui>", then "<ui>Create user</ui>".
server.i4: Open the new user → "Permissions" tab → "Add permissions" → "Create inline policy" → "JSON" tab. Replace the content with the policy below, click "Next", name it OpsWatchAssumeRole, then click "Create policy".
server.i5: Open the "<ui>Security credentials</ui>" tab → "<ui>Create access key</ui>" → use case "<ui>Application running outside AWS</ui>" → "<ui>Next</ui>" → "<ui>Create access key</ui>". Copy the "<ui>Access key</ui>" and the "<ui>Secret access key</ui>": the secret is shown only once.
server.i6: In OpsWatch's .env file, set AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY to these two values, and AWS_REGION to your usual region, for example eu-west-1. Check that OPSWATCH_SECRET holds at least 32 random characters (generate them with openssl rand -base64 48): without it, OpsWatch refuses to start. Then restart OpsWatch with docker compose up -d.
server.profileTitle: Docker: keys in .env, profiles for npm run dev
server.profile: With Docker, put AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in .env. An AWS CLI profile (aws configure --profile opswatch, then AWS_PROFILE=opswatch) is meant for npm run dev: the container runs as user 1001 and usually cannot read a mounted ~/.aws/credentials file, whose mode is 600, and SSO profiles also need a writable cache. If the two key variables and AWS_PROFILE are all set, OpsWatch uses the keys and logs a warning at startup.
server.i7: Check: once you have created the connection in step 1, its page no longer warns that OpsWatch has no AWS identity. The "{identityTitle}" card shows the ARN of the opswatch user.

aws.i1: ECS: open the task definition and note the "<ui>Task role</ui>" (not the "<ui>Task execution role</ui>"). EC2: open the instance → "<ui>Security</ui>" tab → note the "<ui>IAM Role</ui>". If there is none, create a role for the ECS task or the EC2 service and attach it.
aws.i2: Open IAM → Roles → that role → "Add permissions" → "Create inline policy" → "JSON". Paste the policy below, click "Next", name it OpsWatchAssumeRole, then click "Create policy".
aws.i3: Redeploy the ECS service ("Update service" → "Force new deployment") or restart OpsWatch on the instance so it picks up the role. There are no keys to configure: leave AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and AWS_PROFILE empty.

sso.title: What about IAM Identity Center (SSO)?
sso.body: Use IAM, not IAM Identity Center. Identity Center is made for people who sign in: its credentials are temporary and expire after a few hours, so OpsWatch would stop working until someone runs aws sso login again. For a tool that runs all the time, use an IAM user or an ECS or EC2 role. For a quick local try, an SSO profile set through AWS_PROFILE works until the session expires.

ownKey.title: Why not use my own access key?
ownKey.body: It works, but it is not recommended. Your key usually has administrator rights: if OpsWatch's .env, server or database leaks, the whole account is exposed. The dedicated identity can only assume {rolePattern} roles, which are read-only. You can revoke it without touching your own access, and CloudTrail shows clearly what OpsWatch did. Never create access keys for the root user.

s1.title: Create the connection in OpsWatch
s1.purpose: The connection records the account to monitor and generates the unique values its CloudFormation template needs.
s1.i3: Fill in "<ui>{name}</ui>", "<ui>{accountId}</ui>" (the 12 digits of the account to monitor, shown in the account menu at the top right of the AWS console) and "<ui>{regions}</ui>" (the regions where your resources run).
s1.i4: Click "<ui>{submit}</ui>". OpsWatch creates a unique ExternalId and prepares the template for this connection.

s2.title: Deploy the CloudFormation stack in the account to monitor
s2.purpose: The stack creates the read-only role that OpsWatch will assume. Choose one of the three ways below.
s2.region: Create the stack in one region only. IAM is global, so any region works.

console.title: With the AWS console
console.i1: On the OpsWatch connection page, click "<ui>{download}</ui>".
console.i2: In the AWS console of the account to monitor, open <ui>CloudFormation</ui> → <ui>Stacks</ui> → "<ui>Create stack</ui>" → "<ui>With new resources (standard)</ui>".
console.i3: Choose "<ui>Upload a template file</ui>" → "<ui>Choose file</ui>", select the downloaded file, then click "<ui>Next</ui>".
console.i4: In "Stack name", enter {stackName}: the name of the downloaded file without .yaml, also shown in the AWS CLI command of the connection page. Click "Next", then "Next" again.
console.i5: On "<ui>Review and create</ui>", tick "<ui>I acknowledge that AWS CloudFormation might create IAM resources with custom names.</ui>", then click "<ui>Submit</ui>".
console.i6: Wait for the status CREATE_COMPLETE, which takes about one minute.

cli.title: With the AWS CLI
cli.i1: On the connection page, click "<ui>{download}</ui>" and copy the AWS CLI command shown below the button.
cli.i2: Run it from the folder containing the downloaded template, with credentials of the account to monitor. It already contains --capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM, the command-line equivalent of the acknowledgement box.

launch.title: With Launch Stack (experimental)
launch.note: Experimental: this option has not yet been validated against a real AWS account. Only available when OPSWATCH_TEMPLATE_BUCKET is configured. OpsWatch uploads the template to that bucket, so its identity needs s3:PutObject on it, and the console user of the monitored account must be able to read the template object: allow it with a bucket policy granting s3:GetObject on opswatch/templates/*. When in doubt, download the template instead.
launch.i1: On the connection page, click "<ui>{launchStack}</ui>". The AWS console opens with the template and the stack name already filled in.
launch.i2: Tick the acknowledgement box, then click "<ui>Create stack</ui>".

s3.title: Paste the role ARN
s3.purpose: The ARN tells OpsWatch which role to assume in the monitored account.
s3.i1: In CloudFormation, open the stack → "Outputs" tab → copy the value of RoleArn. It looks like {example}.
s3.i2: On the connection page, paste it into "<ui>{roleArnLabel}</ui>" and click "<ui>{save}</ui>".

s4.title: Run the test
s4.purpose: OpsWatch assumes the role and checks, service by service, what it can read.
s4.i1: On the connection page, click "<ui>{run}</ui>". The result appears after a few seconds.
s4.i2: Read the colour of each line:
s4.green: <ui>Green, "{status}"</ui>: OpsWatch can read this service. Nothing to do.
s4.orange: <ui>Orange, "{status}"</ui>: an action is missing and the line says what you lose. Open "<services>{servicesTitle}</services>" to see why OpsWatch needs it, then add it by updating the stack with a newly downloaded template.
s4.red: <ui>Red</ui>: the connection or the check failed, and the message gives the reason. See "<troubleshooting>{troubleshootingTitle}</troubleshooting>".

ambient.title: Running on AWS
ambient.intro: OpsWatch runs on ECS or EC2 in the account it monitors and reads it with its own task or instance role: no stack and no keys.

s1.title: Find the role OpsWatch runs with
s1.purpose: This role will receive the read-only permissions.

s2.title: Attach the read-only policy
s2.i1: Open <ui>IAM</ui> → <ui>Roles</ui> → that role → "<ui>Add permissions</ui>" → "<ui>Create inline policy</ui>" → "<ui>JSON</ui>".

s3.title: Restart OpsWatch
s3.purpose: A restart makes sure OpsWatch runs with the role and its new permissions.
s3.i1: ECS: open the service → "Update service" → "Force new deployment". EC2: restart OpsWatch on the instance, for example with docker compose restart.

s4.title: Create the connection and run the test
s4.purpose: OpsWatch checks that its role can read the account.
s4.i2: Choose "<ui>{method}</ui>". In "<ui>{accountId}</ui>", enter the ID of the account OpsWatch runs in: this method cannot read another account.
s4.i3: Select the regions and click "<ui>{submit}</ui>", then click "<ui>{run}</ui>" on the connection page.

keys.title: With access keys
keys.intro: For a quick local test. The keys belong to a dedicated read-only user, never to your own IAM user or to the root user.

s1.title: Create a dedicated IAM user
s1.purpose: This user can only read, so a leaked key cannot change anything in your account.
s1.i1: In the AWS console of the account to monitor, open <ui>IAM</ui> → <ui>Users</ui> → "<ui>Create user</ui>".
s1.i2: Name it opswatch-readonly and leave "Provide user access to the AWS Management Console" unchecked. Click "Next", "Next" again, then "Create user".

s2.title: Attach the read-only policy
s2.i1: Open the new user → "<ui>Permissions</ui>" tab → "<ui>Add permissions</ui>" → "<ui>Create inline policy</ui>" → "<ui>JSON</ui>" tab.

s3.title: Create an access key
s3.purpose: OpsWatch signs its AWS requests with this key pair.
s3.i1: Open the "<ui>Security credentials</ui>" tab → "<ui>Create access key</ui>" → use case "<ui>Application running outside AWS</ui>" → "<ui>Next</ui>" → "<ui>Create access key</ui>".
s3.i2: Copy the "<ui>Access key</ui>" and the "<ui>Secret access key</ui>". The secret is shown only once.

s4.title: Save the keys in OpsWatch
s4.purpose: OpsWatch encrypts the keys before storing them.
s4.i2: Choose "<ui>{method}</ui>", fill in the name, the account ID and the regions, then click "<ui>{submit}</ui>".
s4.i3: On the connection page, paste the values into "<ui>{accessKeyId}</ui>" and "<ui>{secretAccessKey}</ui>", then click "<ui>{save}</ui>".
s4.i4: The keys are encrypted and never shown again: only a hint like AKIA…MPLE remains.

s5.title: Run the test and look after the key
s5.purpose: A long-lived key needs care for as long as it exists.
s5.i2: Rotate the key regularly: create a new one, save it in OpsWatch, then delete the old one in IAM.
s5.i3: Delete the key in IAM when you stop using OpsWatch, and switch to the <role>IAM role method</role> whenever you can.

GettingStarted.servicesIntro: The role is deliberately narrower than the AWS ReadOnlyAccess policy, which can read the content of S3 buckets. OpsWatch never reads S3, Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store.

pages.title: What OpsWatch shows
pages.intro: Once a connection passes its permission test, pick it in the top bar, then a region, to open these pages.

items.overview: Overview: health summary and automatic insights (tasks below desired over 10 minutes; high CPU or memory, failed deployments, database CPU and memory, Aurora replica lag, load balancer 5xx errors and unhealthy hosts, alarms firing, over 15 minutes).
items.containers: Containers: ECS services with tasks, CPU and memory, then per service its charts, tasks, events, target groups and log groups.
items.databases: Databases: RDS and Aurora instances with their role, metrics and, when Performance Insights is on, the top SQL statements.
items.loadBalancers: Load balancers: requests, 5xx errors, p95 response time and target health of each application load balancer.
items.alarms: Alarms: CloudWatch alarms by state, with target-tracking autoscaling alarms hidden by default.
items.logs: Logs: pick log groups and run CloudWatch Logs Insights queries over up to 24 hours, with example queries for errors, 5xx responses and slow requests.

pages.refresh: Charts cover 1 hour to 7 days and refresh every 2 minutes while the tab is visible; you can pause the refresh.

security.title: Security
security.can1: Read the metadata and metrics of the services listed above.
security.can2: Run the Logs Insights queries you start, which AWS bills.
security.cannot1: Change, create or delete anything in your account.
security.cannot2: Read S3 objects, secrets or parameters.
security.cannot3: Be assumed by any AWS identity other than this OpsWatch instance's: the trust policy names it.
security.externalIdBody: The trust policy already limits the role to this OpsWatch instance's AWS identity, so learning the role ARN is not enough to use it. The ExternalId covers two remaining cases: several OpsWatch instances or tenants sharing one base identity, where one could be pointed at another's role (the confused deputy problem), and a connection configured with the role of another connection. The role only accepts requests that also present the random value generated for its own connection.
security.revokeBody: Delete the CloudFormation stack. The role disappears and OpsWatch loses access immediately. Then remove the connection in OpsWatch.

assumeRole.title: AccessDenied when assuming the role
assumeRole.body: The trust policy does not match: the stack was deployed from an older template, the ExternalId was regenerated, or OpsWatch now runs with another identity. Download the template again and update the stack.

region.title: A region always fails
region.body: The region may be disabled for your account. Enable it in the AWS account settings, or remove it from the connection.

pi.title: Performance Insights is "not applicable"
pi.body: No instance in that region has Performance Insights enabled. Enable it on the database instance to get the top SQL.

scp.title: A permission stays missing although the role has it
scp.body: A service control policy (SCP) of your AWS organization or a permissions boundary may deny the action. Ask your organization administrator.

account.title: The credentials belong to another account
account.body: The role ARN or the keys come from another AWS account than the one entered for the connection. Check the 12-digit account ID.

hub.title: Connect the systems you use
hub.subtitle: OpsWatch reads what you already run and tells you when something is wrong. Start with whichever of these you have.
hub.intro: Most installations begin with AWS, because that is where the services, databases and load balancers are. The others make what OpsWatch finds easier to act on — none of them is required, and each says plainly what it adds.
hub.guidesIntro: Each guide covers what the integration unlocks, what it needs, exactly what OpsWatch is allowed to do with it, and how to take it away again.

unlocks.aws: Services, databases, load balancers, alarms, logs, errors and deployments. This is the monitoring itself.
unlocks.github: Turns a stack frame into a link to the file it came from, and tells you which commits a deployment carried.
unlocks.cloudflare: Traffic, cache and security events at the edge, for the zones you choose.
unlocks.ai: Optional. Lets a model narrate what OpsWatch already measured. Nothing else depends on it.

github.title: Connect GitHub
github.subtitle: So that a problem can tell you what changed.
github.chainLabel: How a problem reaches the code that caused it

0.title: Service
0.detail: An ECS service OpsWatch already watches.

1.title: Repository
1.detail: You map the service to the repository that builds it.

2.title: Deployment
2.detail: The collector records each rollout of that service.

3.title: Commit
3.detail: OpsWatch reads the commits between one rollout and the last.

4.title: Changed files
4.detail: Paths and line counts for each of those commits.

5.title: Problem
5.detail: A problem that opened after the rollout is shown beside it, with the gap stated.

unlocks.title: What connecting GitHub adds
unlocks.intro: Without it, OpsWatch can tell you a service broke twelve minutes after a deployment. With it, it can also tell you which commits that deployment carried and which files they touched — and link a stack frame to the file it came from.

before.title: Before you start
before.intro: Two things, and neither is a surprise later.
before.needDetail: A GitHub account that can see the repositories your services are built from, and permission to create a fine-grained personal access token for them.
before.costDetail: Nothing. OpsWatch makes a handful of read requests per deployment, bounded at ten commits and twenty files each, and stores the result so a page never calls GitHub.

permissions.title: What OpsWatch is allowed to do
permissions.intro: Read your repositories. That is the whole of it.
permissions.grantDetail: Contents: Read and Metadata: Read, scoped to the repositories you want OpsWatch to know about. Nothing else is needed and nothing else is used.
permissions.whyDetail: Metadata names the repository and its default branch, so a link points at the right place. Contents reads the commit list and the files each commit changed. Neither can alter anything.
permissions.guaranteeTitle: Why read-only is more than a promise here
permissions.guaranteeDetail: OpsWatch's GitHub client contains no write request — not a create, not an update, not a delete. A token that happens to carry write permission would still only ever be used to read, because there is no code that could do otherwise. A test asserts that absence, so it cannot quietly change.

steps.title: Connecting it
steps.methodIntro: Five steps, and you can stop after the third — a verified token already links stack frames to files.

token.title: Create a fine-grained token in GitHub
token.purpose: A fine-grained token is scoped to the repositories you pick, so OpsWatch cannot see the rest of your account.
token.body: In GitHub, open Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens, and create one. Choose only the repositories your services are built from, and set Repository permissions → Contents to Read-only and Metadata to Read-only. Copy the token: GitHub shows it once.

store.title: Paste it into OpsWatch
store.purpose: It is encrypted before it is stored, with a key derived for this purpose alone.
store.body: Open Settings → Repositories and paste the token. It is never sent back to your browser afterwards — the field stays empty, and leaving it empty keeps whatever is already stored. An AI key or an AWS credential cannot be decrypted by the same derivation, so one leak is not all of them.

verify.title: Verify it
verify.purpose: A saved token is not a working token, and OpsWatch will not pretend otherwise.
verify.body: Press Verify token. OpsWatch asks GitHub who the token belongs to and shows the account name. Until it does, the connection reads "Saved, not verified" everywhere it appears.

discover.title: Find your repositories
discover.purpose: So you pick from what exists rather than typing an owner and a name.
discover.body: Press Find repositories. OpsWatch lists what the token can see, with the default branch GitHub reports for each. Tick the ones you want recorded and save. The branch matters: a repository recorded against a branch that does not exist builds links to files nobody can open.

map.title: Map a service to a repository
map.purpose: This is the link that turns a deployment into a list of commits.
map.body: Open a problem on the service, or its error detail, and accept the repository OpsWatch suggests — or correct it. Mapping is never applied automatically: a wrong mapping sends somebody to the wrong diff during an incident, which is worse than no mapping at all.

states.title: What good and not-quite-right look like
states.intro: The Integrations page, the Accounts page and this guide all read the same state, so they cannot disagree.
states.goodDetail: The token is verified and at least one repository is recorded. Deployment details start listing commits on the next collector cycle, and stack frames link to files at the commit the error followed.
states.degradedDetail: Usually a token that has never been verified, or repositories recorded without a token. The second is a real, useful state: links to files work and file contents do not, and the page says which.

failures.title: When it does not work
failures.intro: OpsWatch never shows you GitHub's own error text — it can quote your token back — so it names the cause in its own words.

unauthorized.title: GitHub refused the token
unauthorized.fix: It has expired, been revoked, or was pasted incompletely. Create a new one and replace it; the old one is deleted when you do.

forbidden.title: The token is valid but lacks a permission
forbidden.fix: Add Contents: Read and Metadata: Read to the token's repository permissions. OpsWatch tells this apart from a rate limit, because they are fixed differently.

rateLimited.title: GitHub is rate-limiting the token
rateLimited.fix: Wait a few minutes. OpsWatch reads at most ten commits per deployment and five deployments per cycle, so this is usually another tool sharing the token.

noRepositories.title: Find repositories returns nothing
noRepositories.fix: The token is scoped to no repository, or to repositories the account cannot see. Edit its Repository access in GitHub.

wrongBranch.title: File links open a 404
wrongBranch.fix: The repository is recorded against a branch that does not exist. Re-run Find repositories: OpsWatch records the default branch GitHub reports rather than one you typed.

manage.title: Changing or removing it later
manage.intro: Everything is reversible from Settings → Repositories.
manage.disconnectDetail: The token is deleted, not flagged — a row kept with its secret would be something you asked OpsWatch to forget and it did not. Your repositories and mappings stay, because links to files and service mapping work without a token. Reconnect by pasting a new one.

cloudflare.title: Connect Cloudflare
cloudflare.subtitle: So that what happens at the edge is part of the picture.
cloudflare.chainLabel: How a Cloudflare connection is made

0.title: Token
0.detail: You create a read-only API token in Cloudflare and paste it here.

1.title: Verification
1.detail: OpsWatch asks Cloudflare whether the token works, and says so.

2.title: Zones
2.detail: It lists the zones the token can see.

3.title: Your choice
3.detail: Only the zones you tick are read. Nothing else is touched.

unlocks.title: What connecting Cloudflare adds
unlocks.intro: OpsWatch sees your infrastructure from the inside. Cloudflare sees what reached it. Connecting the two is how a quiet load balancer and a spike in blocked requests stop being separate stories.

before.title: Before you start
before.intro: One token, and a decision about scope.
before.needDetail: A Cloudflare account with at least one zone, and permission to create an API token for it.
before.costDetail: Nothing. The reads are within Cloudflare's included API allowance, and OpsWatch reads only the zones you choose.

permissions.title: What OpsWatch is allowed to do
permissions.intro: Read the zones you pick. It cannot change a setting, purge a cache or edit a rule.
permissions.grantDetail: Zone → Zone → Read, and Zone → Analytics → Read, scoped to the zones you want watched. No write permission is needed.
permissions.whyDetail: Zone: Read names your zones so you can choose from a list instead of pasting an identifier. Analytics: Read is what traffic, cache and security-event figures come from.
permissions.guaranteeDetail: The token carries the permissions you gave it, and OpsWatch then reads only the zones you ticked here. A token that can see forty zones does not put forty zones on a page — that would show somebody else's traffic to a reader who never asked for it.

steps.title: Connecting it
steps.methodIntro: Five steps. Nothing is read until the last one.

token.title: Create an API token in Cloudflare
token.purpose: Scoped to the zones you want OpsWatch to see, and to reading them.
token.body: In Cloudflare, open My Profile → API Tokens → Create Token, and start from a custom token. Add Zone → Zone → Read and Zone → Analytics → Read, then set Zone Resources to the specific zones you want watched. Copy the token: Cloudflare shows it once.

store.title: Paste it into OpsWatch
store.purpose: It is encrypted before it is stored, with a key derived for this purpose alone.
store.body: Open Settings → Cloudflare and paste the token. It is never sent back to your browser — the field stays empty afterwards. The derivation is Cloudflare's own, so a code path handling an AWS credential or an AI key cannot read it.

verify.title: Verify it
verify.purpose: A saved token is not a working token.
verify.body: Press Verify token. OpsWatch asks Cloudflare whether it is live and records the answer. Until it passes, the connection reads "Saved, not verified" on every page that mentions it.

discover.title: Find your zones
discover.purpose: So you choose from what exists rather than pasting a zone identifier.
discover.body: Press Find zones. OpsWatch lists what the token can see, with each zone's status. If the list is empty, the token is scoped to no zone — edit its Zone Resources in Cloudflare.

choose.title: Choose what to read
choose.purpose: This is the step that decides what OpsWatch actually looks at.
choose.body: Tick the zones you want and save. Until at least one is ticked the connection is verified and reads nothing, and OpsWatch says exactly that rather than claiming to be connected. Changing the selection later never disturbs the token.

states.title: What good and not-quite-right look like
states.intro: The same state appears on this guide, the Integrations page and the Accounts page. They read one source.
states.goodDetail: The token is verified and at least one zone is chosen. The connection is ready for the edge figures as they land.
states.degradedDetail: Either the token has never been verified, or it is verified and no zone is chosen. The second reads nothing at all, which is why it is not called connected.

failures.title: When it does not work
failures.intro: Cloudflare's own error text never reaches OpsWatch's pages — it can quote a token's identifier — so failures are named in OpsWatch's words.

unauthorized.title: Cloudflare refused the token
unauthorized.fix: It has expired, been rolled, or was pasted incompletely. Create a new one and replace it.

forbidden.title: The token is valid but lacks a permission
forbidden.fix: Add Zone → Analytics → Read. OpsWatch distinguishes this from a rate limit, because waiting will not fix it.

rateLimited.title: Cloudflare is rate-limiting the token
rateLimited.fix: Wait a few minutes. If it persists, another tool is probably sharing the token.

noZones.title: Find zones returns nothing
noZones.fix: The token's Zone Resources are set to no zone, or to zones this account cannot see. Edit them in Cloudflare and verify again.

nothingAppears.title: Connected, but no figures yet
nothingAppears.fix: Check that a zone is ticked. A verified token with no zone selected reads nothing, and the connection says so rather than looking healthy.

manage.title: Changing or removing it later
manage.intro: Everything is reversible from Settings → Cloudflare.
manage.disconnectDetail: The token and the zone selection are deleted together. Nothing is kept "for the history" — a stored secret you asked OpsWatch to forget would be a secret it did not forget. Reconnect by pasting a new token.

ai.title: Connect an AI provider
ai.subtitle: Optional. OpsWatch is complete without one.

0.title: Observed evidence
0.detail: What OpsWatch recorded, with timestamps. Never inferred.

1.title: Correlations
1.detail: Two recorded facts close together, with the gap stated. Never a cause.

2.title: AI hypothesis
2.detail: A guess from a model, labelled as one, beside the evidence it used.

3.title: Suggested investigation
3.detail: What would settle it, so you can check rather than believe.

unlocks.title: What connecting a provider adds
unlocks.intro: A model that can read what OpsWatch already measured and say it in a sentence. It does not measure anything, decide anything, or change anything — grouping, severity, baselines and anomalies are computed by written formulas whether or not a provider is configured.

before.title: Before you start
before.intro: An account with one of the supported providers, and a decision about whether you want this at all.
before.needDetail: An API key from Anthropic or OpenAI, or the address of any endpoint that speaks the OpenAI chat format — including one you host yourself.
before.costDetail: Your provider's usual per-token charge, and only when somebody asks a question. Nothing runs on a schedule. A connection test costs a single token.

permissions.title: What OpsWatch sends, and what it does not
permissions.intro: Your question, and a bounded pack of evidence it already collected.
permissions.grantDetail: The eight worst open problems, five recent deployments, five error groups that changed, and how each family looks — over the last 24 hours, capped at 32 kB. Titles, counts and timestamps.
permissions.whyDetail: No database dump, no raw log lines, no AWS credentials, no account identifiers, and nothing outside the environment you asked about. The limits are applied when the pack is built, not checked afterwards.
permissions.guaranteeTitle: What the model is told it may not do
permissions.guaranteeDetail: Never state a number, a service or a time that is not in the evidence. Never say one thing caused another — only that two happened close together, and how close. Say when the evidence does not support an answer. It is reading your estate, not changing it: OpsWatch has no write access to your infrastructure or your code.

steps.title: Configuring it
steps.methodIntro: Five steps, and you can undo all of them with one button.

choose.title: Choose a provider
choose.purpose: So swapping later is a setting rather than a rewrite.
choose.body: Anthropic and OpenAI are configured by name. The third option, an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, is for a gateway or a model you host yourself — you supply the address, over https.

key.title: Paste your API key
key.purpose: It is the only credential this needs.
key.body: Open Settings → AI provider and paste it. Leaving the field empty keeps whatever is already stored, which is how you change the model without retyping the key.

store.title: How it is stored
store.purpose: So you know what an attacker would have to reach.
store.body: Encrypted with a key derived for this purpose alone, and never sent back to your browser. The function that builds a request to your provider is not given the key at all, so a proxy that logs request bodies cannot capture it.

test.title: Test the connection
test.purpose: A saved key is not a working key.
test.body: Press Test connection. OpsWatch makes a one-token call and records the result as connected, invalid or unavailable. Until it passes, the provider reads "Saved, not tested" everywhere — and Ask OpsWatch stays unavailable, because a capability is what you can use rather than what is stored.

ask.title: Ask a question
ask.body: Open Overview → Ask OpsWatch in any environment. The answer appears under a heading that calls it a hypothesis, with the problems, deployments and error groups it was built from listed beneath it, and the model named. If OpsWatch has not read the environment yet it refuses to ask rather than getting a confident answer about an estate nobody has looked at.

states.title: What good and not-quite-right look like
states.intro: This guide, the Integrations page and the Accounts page read the same state.
states.goodDetail: The key has been tested and passed. Ask OpsWatch appears at the end of the Overview menu, after every deterministic surface.
states.degradedDetail: A key is saved but untested, or its last test failed. Changing the model or the endpoint also returns it here: that is a different connection, and the old result says nothing about it.

failures.title: When it does not work
failures.intro: Your provider's own error text never reaches an OpsWatch page — some providers echo the key back in it — so failures are named in OpsWatch's words.

unauthorized.title: The provider refused the key
unauthorized.fix: Check it, or paste a new one. This also appears if OPSWATCH_SECRET changed since the key was stored, which makes it undecryptable: store it again.

rateLimited.title: The provider is rate-limiting the key
rateLimited.fix: Wait, or use a key with more headroom. OpsWatch sends one request per question and never runs one on a schedule.

refusedEndpoint.title: OpsWatch refused to call the address
refusedEndpoint.fix: A custom endpoint that resolves inside your network or to the cloud metadata service is refused before the request is made, and again on every redirect. Use a public https address.

noEvidence.title: "There is nothing to answer from"
noEvidence.fix: The collector has not read that environment yet. This is deliberate: asking a model anyway would produce a confident paragraph about an estate nobody has looked at.

timeout.title: The provider did not answer in time
timeout.fix: Thirty seconds is the limit. A very large model behind a slow gateway can exceed it; try a smaller one.

manage.title: Changing or removing it later
manage.intro: Everything is reversible from Settings → AI provider.
manage.disconnectDetail: The key is deleted and the provider forgotten. Ask OpsWatch disappears from the menu and every other page works exactly as it did — which is the point of AI being optional rather than merely switchable.

Without keys, an AWS_PROFILE set in the shell that starts OpsWatch must name a profile that exists and can be read.
hints.ExpiredToken: The credentials have expired. Replace the temporary keys (with their AWS_SESSION_TOKEN), or run aws sso login again for an SSO profile, then restart OpsWatch.

ai.title: Connect an AI provider
ai.summary: Optional. It narrates evidence OpsWatch already collected — it never produces the facts.
ai.what: With a model connected, OpsWatch can offer a hypothesis about a problem and answer questions in Ask OpsWatch. The model is given a bounded pack of evidence OpsWatch measured. It does not query your database, it does not read raw logs, and nothing it says becomes a fact.

before.0: An API key from a provider you already use.
before.1: A decision about sending evidence to a third party. OpsWatch is complete without this.

0.title: Add the provider
0.body: Settings, then AI provider. Choose the provider and model and paste the key. It is encrypted before it is stored and never returned to a browser.

1.title: Test the connection
1.body: A saved key is not a working one. The test calls the provider and reports what came back.

2.title: Use it from a problem
2.body: The hypothesis appears under its own heading, after the measured evidence, and is labelled as a hypothesis everywhere it appears.

3.title: Turn it off whenever you like
3.body: Disconnecting deletes the stored key. Every measured page keeps working exactly as before.

ai.verify: The connection test passes and the Integrations page shows the provider as connected with its model named.

0.q: What exactly is sent to the provider?
0.a: A bounded pack: the problem, its measured values, the correlated deployments and error groups. Not your logs, not your database, not your credentials.

1.q: Can the model change a verdict?
1.a: No. Severities, thresholds and states are computed by OpsWatch. The model only ever adds a labelled hypothesis beside them.

2.a: No. It is off by default and everything else works without it.

alarms.title: Alarms, and how they differ from problems
alarms.summary: A CloudWatch alarm is your rule. An OpsWatch problem is what OpsWatch measured. Both matter.
alarms.what: OpsWatch reads every CloudWatch alarm in the account and region you are looking at, and shows what each one watches rather than what it is called. It never changes an alarm, and it never treats one as a problem of its own.

before.0: A connected AWS account whose permission test passes.
before.1: At least one CloudWatch alarm. OpsWatch creates none.

0.title: Read the summary first
0.body: The bar at the top counts every alarm by state. In alarm, OK, and insufficient data are three separate counts — an alarm AWS could not evaluate is never added to OK.

1.title: Narrow by state, then by service
1.body: The state tabs and the service chips are links, so a filtered view can be shared and the back button works. Services come from the alarm’s namespace, never from its name.

2.title: Read a row
2.body: Each row leads with what is watched and where — “CPU on redis-prod” — and keeps the AWS alarm name underneath, because that is what your runbook and the console say.

3.title: Open one
3.body: The detail page explains the condition in full: metric, statistic, threshold, period, how many datapoints must breach, and what AWS does when data is missing.

alarms.verify: The counts at the top add up to the number of alarms you have, and every row names a metric and a resource rather than only an alarm name.

0.q: What is the difference between an alarm and a problem?
0.a: An alarm is a rule somebody wrote in AWS: a threshold on a metric. A problem is something OpsWatch decided was worth your attention, using its own detectors and evidence. An alarm in ALARM state does open a problem — but OpsWatch will never invent causes for it, because the rule is yours and it never saw your reasoning.

1.q: Why can I not see the alarm’s history?
1.a: Reading state transitions needs cloudwatch:DescribeAlarmHistory, which the read-only role does not ask for. Adding it would mean a new template version and every installation redeploying, so it is not granted for one page.

2.a: Target-tracking alarms fire as part of normal autoscaling. Counting them would make every scaling estate look permanently alarmed, so they are excluded until you ask for them.

3.q: The value shown is not the current value.
3.a: It is the datapoint AWS quoted when it last changed the state, which may be hours old. OpsWatch labels it as what AWS reported and does not pay for a second metric call to guess at “now”.

alerts.title: Alerts and notifications
alerts.summary: Rules turn problems into notifications, with a cooldown so nobody is paged twice.
alerts.what: A problem is something OpsWatch measured. An alert rule decides which problems are worth telling somebody about, and where to send them.

before.0: At least one connected account producing problems.

0.title: Look at the rules you already have
0.body: Alert rules. OpsWatch ships a starting set, and a rule you delete stays deleted even when a later version adds new ones.

1.title: Understand the cooldown
1.body: A rule that has fired will not fire again for the same subject until its cooldown passes. A flapping service does not become a flapping phone.

2.title: Acknowledge means a person has seen it
2.body: It stops the noise. It does not close the problem — only three consecutive clear readings do that.

3.title: Choose a destination
3.body: Settings, then Notifications. A webhook posts a signed JSON body to a URL you control. The page tells you what it will send and lets you send a test before you rely on it.

alerts.verify: Send a test notification from the destination you configured and confirm it arrives. The audit log records that it was sent.

0.q: What exactly is in the webhook body?
0.a: The problem, its severity, its subject and a link back into OpsWatch. Never a credential. The settings page shows an example payload.

1.a: OpsWatch retries with a backoff and records the failure. A destination that keeps failing is shown as failing rather than quietly dropped.

2.q: How do I verify a webhook really came from OpsWatch?
2.a: Each request is signed with the shared secret shown when you create the destination. Verify the signature before you act on the body.

aws-permissions.title: AWS permissions: what OpsWatch reads, and what it cannot do
aws-permissions.summary: Every action in the policy, why it is there, and how to change your mind.
aws-permissions.what: The role OpsWatch asks for contains read actions only. This is the list, grouped the way the permission test groups it, so you can check the two against each other.

0.title: Describe calls: what exists
0.body: ECS, EC2, load balancers and RDS describe actions tell OpsWatch which resources you have. They return configuration, never data.

1.title: CloudWatch: what they are doing
1.body: GetMetricData and ListMetrics read the metrics AWS already publishes. ListMetrics is also how OpsWatch discovers Redis and Kubernetes without asking for more permissions. GetMetricData is the one AWS bills for, and OpsWatch caps how often it runs.

2.title: Logs: only when you ask
2.body: Log groups are listed so you can pick one. Queries run when you run them, and the cost is stated beside the button.

3.title: Changing your mind
3.body: Update the stack from the connection page. OpsWatch tells you when the template it generated has moved on from the one you deployed.

aws-permissions.verify: Run the permission test on the connection. Every service you expect shows as allowed; anything else is named with the exact action.

0.q: I want to grant less than the template asks for.
0.a: You can. Remove the actions you do not want and redeploy — the permission test will show those services as denied, and the pages that need them will say so rather than showing you an empty screen.

1.q: Does OpsWatch store my AWS credentials?
1.a: For a role, there is nothing to store: OpsWatch assumes the role each time. For access keys, they are encrypted with your OPSWATCH_SECRET and never returned to a browser.

checkup.title: Checkup: what is worth fixing
checkup.summary: A review of configuration, separate from the problems that are happening now.
checkup.what: Checkup looks at how your estate is set up rather than at what it is doing. It finds the things that will bite later — a service with one task, a database with no backups configured, telemetry that is switched off.

before.0: A connected AWS account that has passed its permission test.

0.title: Open Checkup
0.body: Overview, then Checkup. It reads what it already collected, so it costs nothing to open.

1.title: Read a finding
1.body: Each one says what it saw, why that matters and what to do. Findings are not problems: nothing is on fire.

2.title: Decide
2.body: Some findings are deliberate choices. OpsWatch does not nag, and it never changes anything.

checkup.verify: Checkup lists findings or says plainly that it has nothing to report — and tells you when it last looked.

0.q: What is the difference between a finding, a problem, an alarm and an error?
0.a: A finding is about configuration. A problem is about behaviour OpsWatch measured. An alarm is a CloudWatch rule you wrote. An error is an exception from your application. They are four different things and OpsWatch keeps them apart.

1.q: Does OpsWatch audit my Google account?
1.a: No. Google is only a way to sign in to OpsWatch. There is no Google audit.

0.label: Keep history, so findings have a baseline

cloudflare.summary: Traffic, cache and threats at the edge, for the zones you choose.
cloudflare.what: Cloudflare sees the requests that never reach your origin: the ones it cached, the ones it blocked, and the ones it could not serve. Connecting it tells you what happened in front of AWS.

before.1: Permission to create an API token on it.

0.body: In your Cloudflare dashboard, create an API token with Zone read and Analytics read for the zones you want. Do not use a global API key.

1.title: Paste it into OpsWatch
1.body: Settings, then Cloudflare. The token is encrypted before it is stored and is never sent back to a browser — not even to the page you pasted it into.

2.title: Verify it
2.body: Verification calls Cloudflare and lists the zones the token can actually read. A saved token is not a working one, and OpsWatch shows the difference.

0.a: OpsWatch shows the error code Cloudflare returned rather than a guess. The usual causes are a token without analytics permission or one scoped to a different zone.

1.q: The numbers are a day behind.
1.a: They are daily rollups from Cloudflare’s analytics. OpsWatch says which day each figure belongs to instead of implying it is live.

2.q: Can I replace the token without losing my zone selection?
2.a: Yes. Replacing the credential keeps the connection; only the token changes, and it is verified again.

connect-aws.summary: A read-only IAM role, deployed by a CloudFormation template OpsWatch generates for you.
connect-aws.what: OpsWatch reads your AWS account through a role it is allowed to assume. The role is read-only, the template that creates it is generated for your account, and you can delete it at any time.

before.0: Permission to deploy a CloudFormation stack in the AWS account.
before.1: The AWS account number, twelve digits.
before.2: Which regions you want OpsWatch to read.

1.body: Access keys are offered for local testing and are marked as such. For anything real, use the role.

2.title: Deploy the template
2.body: Download it or use Launch Stack. It creates one IAM role with one read-only policy, and nothing else. The trust policy names OpsWatch’s own identity and an ExternalId unique to this connection, so the role cannot be assumed through another connection.

3.title: Paste the role ARN
3.body: CloudFormation shows it in the stack outputs. OpsWatch checks that it belongs to the account you entered.

0.a: The ARN you pasted is from a different account number than the one on the connection. Check the twelve digits in the ARN.

1.a: That is fine and OpsWatch will keep working — it simply cannot read those. The checklist names each one so you can decide whether to add it.

2.q: Can OpsWatch change anything in my account?
2.a: No. The policy contains read actions only. It cannot deploy, scale, roll back or delete.

connect-github.title: Connect code
connect-github.summary: From a problem, to the deployment near it, to the commit, to the files that changed.
connect-github.what: When OpsWatch knows which repository a service is built from, it can show you what changed just before a problem started. It reads your code; it never writes to it.

before.0: A GitHub account with access to the repositories you want to link.
before.1: A connected AWS account, so there are services to map to.

0.title: Connect GitHub
0.body: Settings, then Repositories. Paste a token with read access to the repositories you care about. It is encrypted before it is stored and never sent back to a browser.

1.title: Choose repositories
1.body: Discover lists what the token can see. Import the ones you want; the rest are left alone.

2.title: Map a service to a repository
2.body: This is the link that makes the chain work. Without it OpsWatch knows a deployment happened and not what was in it.

3.title: Check deployment enrichment
3.body: Containers, then Deployments. An enriched deployment shows the commits it carried and how many files they touched.

4.title: Open code from a problem
4.body: On a problem with a nearby deployment, "what changed" takes you to the commit and the files. Where an error carries a stack frame, the link goes to that file at that commit.

connect-github.verify: A deployment shows its commits. A problem with a deployment near it offers the changed files. Both say plainly when a mapping is missing instead of showing nothing.

0.a: The service is not mapped to a repository, or the commit it deployed is not in the repository OpsWatch has. The deployment page says which.

1.q: Why do code links point at a commit rather than the branch?
1.a: Because the branch moves. A link to a file on main will point somewhere else next week, and the whole value of the link is that it shows the code as it was when the problem started.

2.q: Does a deployment before a problem mean it caused it?
2.a: No, and OpsWatch never says so. It says a deployment happened eight minutes earlier. That is a correlation, and it is yours to interpret.

ec2.title: Monitor EC2
ec2.summary: Instances by availability zone, coloured by the one signal that means broken.
ec2.what: OpsWatch lists your instances and reads their CloudWatch metrics. It colours an instance by its AWS status check — and deliberately not by CPU.

0.body: Instances, then Overview. Each instance is a tile, grouped by availability zone.

1.title: Understand the colour
1.body: Green means the AWS status check passed. Red means it failed. An outline means the instance is running and publishing no status check, so OpsWatch cannot vouch for it.

2.title: Understand what CPU is not
2.body: A batch host at 95% is doing its job; a web server at 95% may be in trouble. OpsWatch cannot tell which yours is, so CPU is shown, ranked and charted — never turned into a verdict.

3.title: Turn on detailed monitoring for finer data
3.body: Basic monitoring publishes every five minutes. Detailed monitoring publishes every minute and is billed by AWS.

ec2.verify: The host map groups your instances by zone and the summary names any zone where something could not be read.

0.a: No status-check metrics are reaching CloudWatch for them. Check that the instances are genuinely running and that the connection has CloudWatch permissions.

1.q: A stopped instance shows as healthy.
1.a: Stopping an instance is a decision somebody made. OpsWatch says it is stopped and does not treat that as a fault.

0.label: Why an outline is not a red square

ecs.title: Monitor ECS
ecs.summary: Clusters, services and tasks — and how to get the CPU and memory numbers.
ecs.what: OpsWatch reads your ECS clusters and services through the describe actions in the role, and their CPU and memory from CloudWatch. It colours a service by whether its tasks are running, what its utilisation is, and how its last deployment went.

before.0: A connected AWS account with ECS permissions allowed.

0.title: Open the ECS overview
0.body: Containers, then Overview. Every service is a tile, grouped by cluster.

1.title: Check the verdict
1.body: A service is healthy when its tasks are running, its CPU and memory are inside the band, and its last deployment completed. A service deliberately scaled to zero is healthy, not broken.

2.title: Turn on Container Insights if you want more
2.body: Basic CPU and memory arrive without it. Container Insights adds task-level counts and is enabled per cluster in the ECS console or with the CLI.

3.title: Point your logs at CloudWatch
3.body: Use the awslogs driver in your task definition so OpsWatch can search them and find errors.

ecs.verify: The ECS overview shows a verdict, the counts beside it, and the checks it ran — including the CPU and memory figures with the threshold they were compared against.

0.a: The service publishes no utilisation metrics. That is normal for some launch types; OpsWatch lists only the checks that ran rather than inventing a zero.

1.q: A service shows 0 of 2 tasks running.
1.a: Nothing is serving. Look at the service events in the AWS console — the usual causes are an image that cannot be pulled, a failing health check, or no capacity.

0.label: Send logs so errors become problems

first-login.title: First login
first-login.summary: Create the administrator, then decide how people sign in.
first-login.what: The first person to open OpsWatch creates the administrator account. After that the setup page is closed and everybody signs in with a password, or with Google if you configure it.

before.1: A password manager, ideally. The password is not recoverable.

0.title: Create the administrator
0.body: Open OpsWatch and fill in the email and password. This happens once; afterwards the setup page answers "not found".

1.title: Sign in
1.body: Use the email and password you just chose.

2.title: Optionally, turn on Google sign-in
2.body: Set the Google client id, secret and public URL in the environment and restart. Sign-in configuration lives in the environment on purpose: a login provider that could be changed from inside the application would be a way to take the application over.

first-login.verify: You land on Connections. The Integrations page shows Google sign-in as connected if you configured it, and as not configured if you did not.

0.a: There is no reset from inside the product. Stop the container, remove the admin row from the database in the data volume, and start again.

1.q: Is Google sign-in the same as connecting Google Cloud?
1.a: No. It is a way of signing in to OpsWatch. OpsWatch does not read anything from Google.

history.title: Keep history and build baselines
history.summary: Off by default, because it costs money. Here is what turning it on buys.
history.what: OpsWatch answers most questions from what AWS already keeps. Historical collection is for the questions that need yesterday: charts on a problem, baselines, reports and objectives.

before.1: A view on how much CloudWatch querying you are willing to pay for.

0.title: Understand why it is off
0.body: Every collection cycle is a billed CloudWatch call. OpsWatch will not spend your money by default, so it ships with collection off and every page that would use it says so.

1.title: Turn it on
1.body: Settings, then Data and history. Choose an interval. The page states what each interval costs in calls per day.

2.title: Choose retention
2.body: Older points are rolled up rather than kept raw, so the database grows slowly and predictably.

3.title: Wait for a baseline
3.body: Baselines need enough history to be meaningful. Until there is enough, OpsWatch says there is not enough rather than comparing against a number it made up.

4.title: Back it up
4.body: Everything lives in the data volume. Snapshot the volume, and keep your OPSWATCH_SECRET with it — without the secret the stored credentials cannot be read.

history.verify: A problem detail shows a chart of the measured signal instead of the sentence explaining that history is off.

0.a: In SQLite, inside the container’s data volume, on your machine. Nothing is sent anywhere.

1.q: I turned it on and the charts are still empty.
1.a: They fill from the moment you turn it on. OpsWatch does not backfill, because backfilling means paying to re-read a window you did not ask for.

2.q: How do I make OpsWatch keep statistics?
2.a: This is that guide. Turn on historical collection; baselines, reports and objectives all build on it.

install.title: Install OpsWatch
install.summary: One container, one volume, on a machine you control.
install.what: OpsWatch runs as a single container with one data volume. Everything it knows — your connections, your problems, your history — lives in that volume on your machine, and nothing is sent anywhere else.

before.0: A machine with Docker and Docker Compose installed.
before.1: A free port. The examples use 3111.

0.title: Get the compose file
0.body: Clone the repository, or copy docker-compose.yml from it.

1.title: Set the secret
1.body: OPSWATCH_SECRET encrypts every credential OpsWatch stores. Generate one and keep it: if you lose it, the stored credentials cannot be decrypted and you will have to reconnect everything.

2.title: Start it
2.body: The first start creates the database and applies every migration.

3.title: Open it
3.body: It binds to localhost only. To reach it from elsewhere, put it behind an HTTPS reverse proxy and set OPSWATCH_PUBLIC_URL — create your administrator account first.

install.verify: The sign-in page loads and asks you to create an administrator. If you see it, the container is running and the database is ready.

0.a: Check the container is healthy with docker compose ps, then read docker compose logs opswatch. A missing OPSWATCH_SECRET is the usual cause.

1.q: Can I move it to another machine?
1.a: Yes. Copy the data volume and use the same OPSWATCH_SECRET. Without that secret the stored credentials are unreadable.

kubernetes.title: Monitor Kubernetes on EKS
kubernetes.summary: Container Insights is the whole story — what it gives you, and exactly where it stops.
kubernetes.what: OpsWatch reads Kubernetes through CloudWatch Container Insights. That needs no permission beyond the ones your role already has, and it is not on by default: until you enable it, OpsWatch cannot see your cluster and will say so rather than showing you a reassuring empty page.

before.0: An EKS cluster and permission to add an add-on to it.
before.1: A connected AWS account with CloudWatch permissions allowed.
before.2: Container Insights is billed by AWS as custom metrics. Check the cost for your cluster size before enabling it everywhere.

0.title: Enable Container Insights on the cluster
0.body: The simplest route is the CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on, which installs the agent for you.

1.title: Wait for metrics to appear
1.body: The first datapoints arrive within a few minutes. OpsWatch finds clusters by their node-count metric, so nothing appears until that is published.

2.title: Open the Kubernetes section
2.body: Every pod is a tile, grouped by namespace. Nodes and cluster health are beside it.

3.title: Read the boundary
3.body: The page carries a card saying what this view cannot see. It is worth reading once.

kubernetes.verify: The Kubernetes section shows your cluster, its nodes, and a tile for every running pod. If it still says no cluster is reporting, the metrics are not reaching CloudWatch yet.

0.q: It says no cluster is reporting, but I have one.
0.a: Container Insights is not enabled on it, or the agent cannot publish. OpsWatch cannot tell that apart from having no cluster, so it claims neither.

1.q: Why can I not see containers, only pods?
1.a: Container Insights aggregates to the pod. Per-container state lives in the kubelet and would need something running inside your cluster to read it.

2.q: A workload I know is broken does not appear.
2.a: This is the sharpest edge of reading Kubernetes from CloudWatch. A workload whose pods all failed to start publishes no pod metrics, so it looks the same here as a workload that does not exist. Events and pod phases are not in CloudWatch.

3.q: Would an in-cluster agent from OpsWatch fix that?
3.a: It would: events, pod phases, owner references and per-container state all need something inside the cluster. OpsWatch does not ship one. It is a real product with its own trust boundary — something running in your cluster, holding a credential, sending data out — and we will not pretend it exists.

0.label: Why missing telemetry is never green

logs.title: Send logs so OpsWatch can read them
logs.summary: CloudWatch Logs in, search and error grouping out.
logs.what: OpsWatch reads logs from CloudWatch Logs. It searches them when you ask, and it groups exceptions into errors that can become problems.

before.0: A connected AWS account with logs permissions allowed.

0.title: Send your logs to CloudWatch
0.body: On ECS, set the awslogs driver on the container definition. On EC2, install the CloudWatch agent. On Lambda it happens by itself.

1.title: Choose the log groups
1.body: Logs, then Sources. OpsWatch lists what it can see and you opt each group in. Nothing is queried until you do.

2.title: Search
2.body: Logs, then Search. Queries are Logs Insights queries and AWS bills for the data they scan — the estimate is beside the button.

3.title: Let errors group themselves
3.body: OpsWatch fingerprints exceptions by their type, their normalised message and the frames that matter — never by line number, so a blank line inserted above does not split a group in two.

logs.verify: The Errors page lists groups with a count and a first-seen time, and a search returns rows from your chosen groups.

0.a: Either the logs permissions are denied, or nothing is writing to CloudWatch Logs in that region.

1.a: They are billed by data scanned. Narrow the time range and pick fewer groups; OpsWatch shows the estimate before you run one.

0.label: Turn an error into a line of code

problems.title: Problems, from opened to resolved
problems.summary: What a problem is, how it differs from an alarm, and how it closes.
problems.what: A problem is something OpsWatch measured and decided was worth your attention. It opens, it can come back, and it closes only when the measurement says so.

before.0: A connected AWS account with something running in it.

0.title: Read the first line
0.body: What it is, how serious, how long it has been going on, and where. If that line does not answer those four things, tell us.

1.title: Read what it affected
1.body: OpsWatch says "user impact not established" more often than not. That is the honest answer: it measures your estate, not your users.

2.title: Read why it opened
2.body: The measured value, the threshold it crossed, and the value it has to come back under.

3.title: Follow what to check
3.body: Each suggestion carries the evidence that produced it — a deployment eight minutes earlier, an error group that appeared nearby. An empty list is an answer too.

4.title: Let it close itself
4.body: A problem resolves after three consecutive clear readings over at least fifteen minutes. One quiet minute does not close anything.

problems.verify: Open a problem. You should see the verdict, the impact, the rule, what to check, possible causes, and a timeline of when it opened and whether it came back.

0.q: What is the difference between a problem and an alarm?
0.a: An alarm is a CloudWatch rule you wrote. A problem is a rule OpsWatch applied. An alarm in ALARM state becomes a problem, and OpsWatch will not invent causes for it — the rule is yours, not ours.

1.q: What is the difference between acknowledging and resolving?
1.a: Acknowledging says a person has seen it. Resolving is a measurement, and only the measurement can do it.

2.q: It says "Possible causes". Are those findings?
2.a: No. That card is the only thing on the page OpsWatch did not measure. It says so in its own words.

0.label: Connect code, so a problem can point at a commit

reading-status.title: Green, amber, red — and the two that are neither
reading-status.summary: What each colour means, and why OpsWatch refuses to show green it has not earned.
reading-status.what: Every resource OpsWatch shows has one of five states. Three of them are verdicts. Two of them are admissions, and they are the reason you can trust the other three.

before.0: Nothing. This is the one to read first.

0.title: Healthy means checked
0.body: Green says somebody looked, recently, and every check that ran passed. It never means "no problem row exists". The absence of a problem is the absence of evidence, not evidence of health.

1.title: Needs attention and Critical are measured
1.body: Amber and red come from a rule with a number in it. The problem page quotes that number and the threshold it crossed, so you can disagree with it.

2.title: Not evaluated means nobody looked
2.body: An outline with nothing in it. OpsWatch found the resource and has no reading for it — often because the telemetry it needs is not switched on.

3.title: Reading is old means we looked, a while ago
3.body: Same colour, different sentence. The last reading is too old to stand for what is happening now.

reading-status.verify: Open any infrastructure overview. Beside the verdict you will find the counts — how many are healthy, how many are not evaluated — and the list of checks that actually ran, with the age of the reading.

0.a: The telemetry OpsWatch needs is not reaching CloudWatch. Each section says which signal is missing and links to the guide for turning it on.

1.q: Why is a busy resource still green?
1.a: Because busy is not broken. OpsWatch only colours by signals that genuinely mean trouble — a failed status check, a saturated engine, tasks that are not running. High CPU on its own is shown, not judged.

redis.title: Monitor Redis on ElastiCache
redis.summary: Engine CPU, memory, evictions and hit rate — and which of them actually mean trouble.
redis.what: OpsWatch finds your Redis nodes through the metrics they publish to CloudWatch. It needs no ElastiCache permission and no stack redeployment. It judges two signals and shows several more without judging them.

before.0: A connected AWS account with CloudWatch permissions allowed.
before.1: At least one ElastiCache Redis node that has been running long enough to publish metrics.

0.title: Open the Redis section
0.body: Every node is a tile, grouped by cluster. Nothing to configure: if the nodes publish metrics, they are there.

1.title: Engine CPU is the one that matters
1.body: Redis runs its commands on a single thread. A four-core node can sit at 25% CPU with a completely saturated engine, which is why OpsWatch judges engine CPU and not CPU. AWS suggests alarming around 90%; OpsWatch warns at 75%.

2.title: Memory is about what happens next
2.body: As memory usage approaches 100%, Redis starts evicting keys, and past it writes fail. OpsWatch warns at 85% and calls it critical at 95%.

3.title: Evictions are a symptom, not an outage
3.body: A full cache evicting keys is a cache doing its job. OpsWatch warns so that you know, and does not treat it as a failure.

4.title: Hit rate and connections are shown, not judged
4.body: A cache deliberately holding only hot keys can run a low hit rate correctly, and OpsWatch cannot read your connection limit without the ElastiCache API. Both are numbers worth seeing and neither is a verdict.

redis.verify: The Redis section shows your cluster with a tile per node, and the node table shows engine CPU, memory, connections, evictions and hit rate. An idle cache shows no hit rate at all rather than zero per cent.

0.q: No Redis node is publishing metrics.
0.a: OpsWatch finds Redis through its engine CPU metric. A cluster that has just started, or one on an engine version old enough not to publish it, will not appear.

1.q: Engine CPU is high but CPU is low. Which is wrong?
1.a: Neither. That is the normal shape of a saturated Redis on a multi-core node, and it is exactly why the engine metric exists.

2.q: Why can I not see the node type or the replication setup?
2.a: Those come from the ElastiCache API, which is not in the role. OpsWatch reads what your nodes are doing, not what they are.
